paper.title: How simple can you go? An off-the-shelf transformer approach to molecular dynamics
paper.research_summary: This paper presents MD-ET, a minimally modified edge transformer architecture for molecular dynamics (MD) that intentionally omits built-in rotational equivariance and energy conservation—two common physical inductive biases in ML force fields. The model is pretrained on ∼30 × 10⁶ molecular structures from the QCML database using supervised learning to predict forces directly (not via energy gradients), then fine-tuned on benchmark datasets (e.g., MD17, SPICE) to evaluate accuracy, stability, and physical consistency. The study empirically tests whether an 'off-the-shelf' transformer can achieve competitive MD performance without architectural constraints, analyzing its approximate equivariance, approximate energy conservation, and fidelity of NVT/NVE simulations.

task.task_name_raw: molecular dynamics simulation using machine-learned force fields
task.objective: To develop and evaluate a minimally modified, off-the-shelf transformer architecture (MD-ET) for molecular dynamics simulations that achieves competitive accuracy and stability without built-in rotational equivariance or energy conservation.
constraints: no automatic differentiation for force derivation
output_goal: stable NVT and NVE molecular dynamics trajectories

evidence.text: We present a recipe for MD using an edge transformer (ET), an “off-the-shelf” transformer architecture that has been minimally modified for the MD domain, termed MD-ET. Our model implements neither built-in equivariance nor energy conservation.

We aim to use an architecture that could be used in some related ML setting with minimal changes. Our aim is to explore the potential benefits of a fully unconstrained approach to MD while highlighting problems arising from a lack of physical inductive biases.
evidence.section: We examine the effects of forgoing almost all commonly

evidence.text: We use the transformer, an architecture that has proven to scale well in many domains, as a starting point in our design process. Since we want to keep the architecture as close as possible to a regular transformer implementation, we also choose to forgo graph construction and, therefore, cutoffs completely.

stages.stage_goal: Obtain large-scale quantum chemistry reference data spanning the periodic table, including out-of-equilibrium structures and different spin and charge states.

evidence.text: QCML ranges across the periodic table, including out-of-equilibrium structures and different spin and charge states, and includes properties for a subset of ∼30 × 10⁶ entries calculated with density functional theory accuracy at the PBE0 level (including dispersion corrections).
evidence.section: We examine the effects of forgoing almost all commonly

stages.stage_goal: Create train/validation/test splits ensuring conformational integrity and apply random rotations/reflections to learn approximate O(3)-equivariance.

evidence.text: We create an approximate 90%/5%/5% split from QCML. As QCML contains multiple conformations for each structure sampled along its normal modes, we ensure that all conformations of a structure are assigned to the same split. To learn approximate equivariance, we use data augmentation: during pretraining, we duplicate each batch once and apply random rotations and reflections to both copies to form an augmented batch.

stages.stage_goal: Train MD-ET to directly predict atomic forces (not via energy gradients) using supervised learning on QCML.
stage_input: molecular embeddings (spin/charge, atomic numbers, pairwise distances, displacement vectors)

evidence.text: Instead of predicting a combined loss of energies and forces or calculating forces as the negative gradient of the predicted energy with respect to positions, we predict forces directly.
evidence.section: We examine the effects of forgoing almost all commonly

evidence.text: we perform supervised pretraining on the new QCML dataset. [...] We train MD-ET for 880k steps on QCML using a batch size of 1024

stages.stage_goal: Adapt the pretrained MD-ET to specific target molecules or datasets (e.g., MD17, SPICE, xxMD) with minimal additional training.
stage_input: small samples from target datasets (e.g., 1000 CCSD(T) samples, 2000 fine-tuning steps)

evidence.text: For downstream task evaluation, we fine-tune the model for a small number of steps only.
evidence.section: We examine the effects of forgoing almost all commonly

evidence.text: In addition to fine-tuning ET-MD for 2000 steps, which we see as the default way to use a large-scale pretrained model, we also report results for training the model directly on MD17.

stages.stage_name_raw: benchmark evaluation of force prediction accuracy
stages.stage_goal: Quantify force prediction error (MAE/RMSE) on standard datasets (QCML, MD17, Ko2020, xxMD, SPICE).
stage_output: comparisons to SpookyNet, PaiNN, Orb-v2, etc.

evidence.text: In Table I, we present the mean absolute error (MAE) of force predictions for MD-ET, SpookyNet, and PaiNN on the QCML evaluation set at the end of pretraining.

stages.stage_name_raw: NVE and NVT molecular dynamics simulation
stages.stage_goal: Assess physical consistency by running microcanonical (NVE) and canonical (NVT) MD simulations and measuring energy drift, stability time, and observables (e.g., h(r), velocity autocorrelation spectra).

evidence.text: For MD simulations, we evaluate either the pretrained model without further training (zero-shot) or fine-tune using a small number of samples of the target structure (few-shot).
evidence.section: We examine the effects of forgoing almost all commonly

evidence.text: We find that NVE simulations with MD-ET are approximately energy-conserving for some small systems, but with increasing system size, the total energy tends to increase with time (see Fig. 3).
evidence.section: C. Unconstrained models can learn to approximately conserve energy without explicit inductive biases

stages.stage_goal: Quantify deviation from rotational equivariance (Eeq) and energy conservation (antisymmetric ratio λ) using analytical metrics and visual diagnostics.
